tldr: We achieved cooperative control for a shipboard robotic arm catching a drone in mid-air under severe wind and deck motion using curriculum reinforcement learning with an intelligent adversarial wind agent. Even in unseen, severe sea states, the method reduced crash rates by up to 14% compared to conventional domain randomization, demonstrating exceptional robustness.
hero_caption: Training flowchart of the proposed method (HARL-AC). The cooperative drone-arm team (Team A) faces an adversarial agent controlling wind and waves (Team B). Stable training is achieved through a bidirectional curriculum that maintains a 30% adversary win rate alongside staged difficulty progression.
overview:
Landing a drone on the deck of a small vessel is notoriously difficult due to ship motion, wind gusts, and deck-induced air turbulence. The traditional approach—hovering at low altitude and cutting motor power to drop the craft—runs the persistent risk of gusts blowing the drone off the deck or causing severe damage. In this work, the authors focus on a "mid-air capture" approach, where a ship-mounted robotic arm catches the drone directly while in flight.

To coordinate two systems with vastly different dynamics—a drone and a robotic arm—the authors adopt Heterogeneous-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (HAPPO). However, standard domain randomization (DR) struggles to expose agents to worst-case boundary disturbances, leaving them vulnerable to sudden real-world shifts. Conversely, simply adding an adversary that maximizes disturbance creates unsolvable tasks early on, causing training to collapse.

To tackle this challenge, the authors propose HARL-AC, introducing an adversarial wind agent governed by a bidirectional curriculum. This mechanism dynamically scales Dryden turbulence intensity to maintain the adversary's win rate at around 30%. Furthermore, they built a coupled ocean dynamic model in simulation, linking wind strength directly to 5-DOF vessel motion via the Pierson-Moskowitz wave spectrum.

Large-scale simulations in NVIDIA Isaac Lab show that on training conditions (Sea States 0, 4, and 5), HARL-AC matches or exceeds domain randomization with success rates up to 97.5%. Its true strength emerges on unseen, severe conditions (Sea States 7, 8, and 10): at Sea State 10, HARL-AC boosts the median success rate by 16% and reduces crash rates by up to 14% compared to domain randomization. Adversarial training steered the policy toward a cautious strategy—stabilizing attitude rather than aggressively fighting gusts—yielding superior generalization.
contributions: Built a heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning system for mid-air drone capture using a shipboard robotic arm, avoiding direct deck landings.
Incorporated a realistic maritime dynamics model into simulation, coupling adversarial wind control directly with wave-induced vessel motion.
Developed HARL-AC, a bidirectional curriculum learning method that dynamically scales turbulence intensity while constraining the adversary's win rate to 30%.
Demonstrated zero-shot robustness in severe, out-of-distribution sea states (Sea States 7–10), lowering crash rates by up to 14% over standard domain randomization.

sections.heading: A safer way to recover drones on swaying ship decks
sections.summary: Maritime deck landings risk aircraft damage due to severe gusts, ship motion, and deck air turbulence. This paper proposes a cooperative control setup where a ship-mounted robotic arm catches a drone in mid-air, evaluating reinforcement learning methods to maximize its disturbance rejection.
sections.details:
Safe landing and recovery are essential hurdles for fully autonomous drone operations. In conventional autonomous landings, drones typically hover close to the surface and cut motor power, dropping onto the deck from a low height. However, on small vessels navigating rough seas, free-falling drones can easily be tossed overboard by sudden gusts or damaged on impact.

To solve this, the authors propose a "mid-air capture" approach using an industrial robotic arm mounted on the deck. Catching the drone in flight avoids deck collisions and ground-effect turbulence, while arm tip motion can actively absorb ship sway. Yet, realizing this requires tight cooperative control between two robots with fundamentally different dynamics.

Standard cooperative multi-agent RL algorithms like MAPPO rely on shared parameters, which restricts representational capacity and causes training instability across asymmetric, heterogeneous agents. Meanwhile, conventional domain randomization (DR) rarely exposes policies to worst-case edge cases, limiting true disturbance tolerance. Building on HAPPO—which guarantees monotonic improvement without parameter sharing—this work introduces HARL-AC, combining an adversarial wind agent with curriculum learning to tackle harsh maritime environments.

sections.heading: Where heterogeneous multi-agent learning meets adversarial curricula
sections.summary: The approach integrates HAPPO to prevent policy degradation in heterogeneous multi-agent setups with separate team-specific critics to avoid value estimation collapse. To keep the adversary from overpowering the agents and halting learning, the method pairs cooperative pre-training with progressive difficulty scaling.
sections.details:
Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) is standard in cooperative multi-agent RL (MARL). However, parameter-sharing approaches like MAPPO fail when handling heterogeneous systems like an arm and a drone. Forcing distinct dynamics into a shared policy oversimplifies representations and impairs convergence. HAPPO solves this by sequentially updating each agent, theoretically guaranteeing monotonic improvement without parameter sharing.

To bridge the reality gap, Robust Adversarial RL (RARL) introduces adversarial disturbances, but naive multi-agent extensions hit a major roadblock. If the cooperative team and the adversarial team share a single critic, value estimates collapse to a zero-sum average regardless of outcome. This erases advantage estimates and causes PPO training to break down. This paper adopts the HARL-A framework, keeping team critics completely separate to avoid vanishing gradients.

Furthermore, an unconstrained adversary makes tasks impossibly hard from the start, causing immediate training failure. While prior research explored student-teacher adversarial curricula and progressive partner difficulty, this paper establishes a framework that balances structured stage progression with real-time adversary difficulty regulation in a cooperative-versus-adversarial setting.

sections.heading: Battling smart winds: HARL-AC architecture and training design
sections.summary: A cooperative team (Team A) of a UR10 arm and a quadcopter faces an adversarial agent (Team B) controlling wind and wave action. A bidirectional curriculum constraining adversary win rates to 30% across four stages keeps training right at the solvable frontier under severe conditions.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Multi-agent formulation
The setup involves three agents across two teams. Team A (the cooperative team) pairs a deck-mounted UR10 robotic arm with an Avular Vertex One quadcopter, aiming to capture the drone using the arm's end-effector (EE). To remain independent of specific gripper hardware, capture success is defined as the drone's base staying within a 0.5 m radius sphere above the EE for 3 seconds while maintaining a speed below 3 m/s. Team B (the adversarial team) consists of the wind agent.

Observation spaces are 23-dimensional for the drone, 37-dimensional for the UR10 arm, and 19-dimensional for the wind agent. Action spaces are 4D for the drone (thrust and 3-axis angular rates), 6D for the arm (target joint positions), and 3D for the wind agent (global wind force vector). The training uses HAPPO, where Team A's critic receives the concatenated 60D joint state, while Team B's critic independently processes its own 19D state.

### 3.2 Adversarial model & Wind-Wave Coupling
The adversary's actions go beyond random noise. Its 3D action vector passes through a tanh function and a low-pass filter to generate a smooth mean wind vector $\vec{\mu}_{\text{wind}}$. Realistic atmospheric fluctuations are added using a discrete-time first-order Markov Dryden turbulence model $\vec{x}_{\text{turb}}$, clamped so the total wind velocity does not exceed the stage limit $V_{\max}$.

A key contribution is "Wind-Wave Coupling." Wind generated by the adversary passes through a filter (time constant 0.5 s) into a sea state parameter $U_t$, driving a Pierson-Moskowitz wave spectrum. Stronger wind triggers realistic 5-DOF vessel motion (surge, sway, heave, roll, and pitch). The adversary can therefore disrupt the quadcopter directly while simultaneously shaking the ship deck to throw off the robotic arm.

### 3.4 & 3.5 Curriculum learning & Bidirectional adversarial curriculum
Training advances through four stages (Stages 0 to 3). Stage 0 pre-trains drone flight with an upright, static arm. Stage 1 activates the arm. Stage 2 introduces the adversarial wind agent, and Stage 3 unlocks maximum wind speeds and full wind-wave coupling. Transitions are governed by exponential moving averages (EMA) of success rates, using asymmetric update rules (slow to promote, fast to demote) to guarantee stability.

To prevent the adversary from creating unsolvable gales, a "bidirectional curriculum" pins the adversary target win rate to $T_{\text{adv}} = 0.30$ (30%). If the adversary wins more than 30% of episodes in a batch, Dryden turbulence intensity $\sigma$ decreases; if lower, $\sigma$ increases. This constraint compels the adversary to discover structural vulnerabilities rather than relying on overwhelming brute force.

captions.F1: HARL-AC system architecture and curriculum progression. Beginning with Stage 0 pre-training, the framework advances to challenging Stage 3 wind-wave coupling guided by EMA success rate monitoring and a 30% adversary win rate target.

sections.heading: Head-to-head with domain randomization: experimental setup
sections.summary: To assess the proposed method, the authors implemented a domain randomization (DR) baseline using pure Dryden turbulence without an adversary. Both policies were trained across 10 random seeds for 250 million steps, evaluating zero-shot generalization on training sea states and unseen severe conditions (Sea States 7, 8, and 10).
sections.details:
### 4.1 Ablation Study: Stochastic Wind with Curriculum (Pure Dryden)
To determine whether adversarial training outperforms standard domain randomization (DR), the authors designed an ablation baseline using stochastic wind. This baseline replaces the adversarial agent with random wind generated by filtering white noise through a Dryden model. Without automated difficulty tuning, turbulence intensity $\sigma$ was fixed at $\sigma=4$ in Stage 2 and $\sigma=7$ in Stage 3.
To avoid overfitting to specific frequencies, the baseline applies a bimodal wind profile combining two stochastic processes: a broad thermal updraft ($L_{\text{slow}}=2.0L$) and rapid micro-turbulence ($L_{\text{fast}}=0.2L$).

### 4.2 Training Instances & 4.3 Evaluation
HARL-AC and the DR baseline were each evaluated across 10 random seeds. Every run executed across 254 parallel environments for 250 million environment steps, taking roughly 6.5 hours to converge. Performance was tracked using three metrics: success rate (percentage of successful captures), crash rate (percentage of drone crashes), and timeout rate (percentage of runs where the drone remained airborne but missed capture within the 5-second limit).

Evaluation included in-distribution testing across training conditions (Sea States 0, 4, and 5) as well as out-of-distribution (OOD) testing to simulate real-world transfer gaps. Specifically, the models were evaluated zero-shot without online adaptation across 20 evaluation runs (10,000 episodes total) on unseen Sea States 7, 8, and catastrophic Sea State 10. A single-environment baseline trained exclusively on Sea State 4 without a curriculum or adversary ("Baseline SS4") served as an additional benchmark.

sections.heading: Standing out in unseen storms: agents learn caution to avoid crashes
sections.summary: DR and HARL-AC posted comparable success rates (up to 97.5%) on training conditions, but HARL-AC achieved a 16% higher success rate and cut crash rates by 14% at unseen Sea State 10. Adversarially trained agents developed a safety-first behavior, intentionally taking more time to stabilize before capture.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Training results
Comparing learning curves, HARL-AC progressed smoothly from early stages, advancing from Stage 2 to Stage 3 in 108 million steps compared to 114 million for DR. The adversary pushed the team to explore diverse state spaces early, helping the cooperative pair discover generalizable recovery behaviors faster.
In Stage 3, HARL-AC exhibited temporary crash rate spikes around 138 million and 159 million steps, accompanied by sharp drops in success rate. This was not policy collapse; rather, the adversarial agent (Team B) discovered novel gust patterns that defeated the team. Team A subsequently adapted and recovered, reflecting healthy adversarial competition. At convergence, DR achieved a slightly higher training success rate (94.3% vs. 90.8%), reflecting the continuous 30% failure pressure maintained by the adversary.

### 5.2 Out-of-distribution evaluation
The true value of the approach surfaced on unseen, extreme sea states (Sea States 7, 8, and 10). On familiar conditions (Sea States 0, 4, and 5), HARL-AC and DR performed similarly (97.5% vs. 95.4% at SS 0; 94.0% vs. 94.3% at SS 5). However, DR performance degraded sharply on severe unseen conditions.
At Sea State 10, DR median success dropped to 45.9%, while HARL-AC maintained 60.0% (a 16% margin). Furthermore, HARL-AC lowered crash rates by 14% compared to DR on both Sea States 8 and 10.

Visual inspection of simulated rollouts explains this performance gap. The DR model acted "reactionary"—it banked heavily to counteract immediate gusts, leaving it vulnerable to sudden wind shifts that caused rapid flips and crashes. In contrast, the HARL-AC model proved "cautious"—it avoided overreacting to gusts, prioritizing attitude stabilization before attempting an approach.
As a consequence of this caution, HARL-AC experienced slightly higher timeout rates than DR (<3%). However, in real maritime operations, arriving 2 to 3 seconds late is negligible. Choosing to wait a few seconds for safe capture rather than rushing into a crash represents the key operational advantage delivered by the adversarial curriculum.

captions.F2: Success, crash, and timeout rates across training. Vertical lines indicate curriculum stage transitions. In Stage 3, the adversarial model (blue) experiences temporary crash spikes as the adversary finds new attack strategies, but successfully adapts and completes training.
captions.F3: Success rate (left) and crash rate (right) across sea states. While performance is comparable on training sea states (SS 0, 4, 5), HARL-AC (blue) retains markedly higher success and lower crash rates on unseen severe sea states (SS 7, 8, 10) compared to DR (orange) and single-environment baselines (yellow).
captions.F4: Comparison of timeout rates across sea states. While timeouts remain low overall (<3%), HARL-AC (blue) exhibits slightly higher rates than DR, reflecting its trade-off of prioritizing attitude stability over speed.

sections.heading: Wrapping up: the power of adversarial training for harsh real-world settings
sections.summary: In mid-air drone capture via a shipboard robotic arm, curriculum reinforcement learning with an adversarial wind agent (HARL-AC) showed superior generalization and disturbance rejection over standard domain randomization. Learning cautious, safety-first policies provides a promising path toward bridging challenging sim-to-real gaps.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated the effectiveness of adversarial heterogeneous multi-agent RL (HARL-AC) on a highly dynamic maritime recovery task.

By continuously exploiting weaknesses during training, the adversary forced the cooperative team to explore broader state spaces and develop fundamental recovery skills. This produced a cautious landing policy that prioritizes attitude stability over raw speed. When subjected to violent, unseen conditions (Sea State 10), the policy achieved up to a 16% higher success rate and a 14% lower crash rate than domain randomization.

Real maritime conditions frequently violate simulation assumptions. In such uncertain domains, training against an adversary operating at the solvable frontier encourages natural safety margins—making this a powerful paradigm for physical deployments.

takeaways: Domain randomization (DR) handles average disturbances well but often misses worst-case conditions; adversarial training provides superior zero-shot generalization in severe out-of-distribution (OOD) settings.
To prevent adversarial multi-agent training from collapsing, a bidirectional curriculum that dynamically regulates turbulence to maintain an adversary win rate target (30% here) is highly effective.

Coordinating heterogeneous robots (such as an aerial drone and a stationary arm) requires sequential policy updates without parameter sharing via HAPPO, alongside separate critic networks for each team.
Adversarial training nudges policies toward cautious behavior—prioritizing balance and waiting for stability rather than rushing—which strongly benefits real-world, safety-critical tasks.
limitations: All experiments were conducted in simulation (NVIDIA Isaac Lab); no physical sim-to-real transfer was validated on real UR10 arms or quadcopters.

Capture detection was abstracted into a geometric and velocity criterion (remaining within a target sphere for 3 seconds), omitting contact dynamics, impact forces, and grasping mechanisms of physical grippers or nets.
Cautious approach strategies increase capture times by 2 to 3 seconds compared to DR, posing potential operational trade-offs during critical, low-battery emergencies.
